question: How did Bach begin to influence classical music?
reference:
Not really Mozart, Haydn, Schubert but later

Barely even Beethoven. 1829 died.

Big Picture

• During Bach’s lifetime and right after, his music was mostly seen as pedagogical and religious, not fashionable.

• His influence was transmitted primarily through:

• His sons—C.P.E. Bach especially, who was a key figure in the transition from Baroque to Classical.

• Pedagogical works—The Well-Tempered Clavier became a foundation for keyboard study.

• Mendelssohn’s revival—In 1829, Mendelssohn famously staged St. Matthew Passion, kicking off the “Bach revival” that cemented his influence on Romantic composers like Brahms.

question: How does polis work?
reference: Phase 1: agenda setting via "listening at scale," using an open source tool called Polis. oversimplified description is you: (i) open a conversation about a topic (how to make SF more kid-friendly) and then let people write statements. (ii) people can upvote statements, but not respond directly, so it avoids antagonistic threads (iii) clusters start to emerge.. cluster means a set of people who are roughly agreeing on an answer set across a variety of questions (iv) each cluster is counted as one vote (so not one person one vote) and only statements that have support from a super majority of clusters get put on the agenda (v) over the open period of the polis conversation, people can tweak statements to earn support from more clusters, thus finding rough consensus and tipping over into super majority support. The output of that process is an agenda with a set of statements, maybe one being, "we need more spaces in the city that prioritize people over cars." Then Phase 2: there is a meeting of the actual stakeholders involved in the decision (e.g. small biz owners, the city, museums, etc.) and they have a livestreamed open policy-making session, working only off the agenda items.

question: When did voluntary national education standards in the US fall apart?
reference:

1994, when Lynne V. Cheney attacked the not-yet-released history standards for their political bias. As chairperson of the National Endowment for the Humanities, Cheney had funded the development of these standards along with the Department of Education. Her scathing critique in the Wall Street Journal opened up a bitter national argument about what history, or rather, whose history, should be taught.

Cheney lambasted the standards as the epitome of left-wing political correctness, charging that they emphasized the nation’s failings while paying scant attention to its great men. The standards document, she said, mentioned Joseph McCarthy and McCarthyism nineteen times, the Ku Klux Klan seventeen times, and Harriet Tubman six times, while mentioning Ulysses S. Grant just once and Robert E. Lee not at all. Nor was there any reference to Paul Revere, Alexander Graham Bell, Thomas Edison, Jonas Salk, or the Wright brothers. question:
Cities in pre-Industrial Europe:

Fernand Braudel, The Structures of Everyday Life
reference:
Yes, dirty. But growth happens in towns

Towns, cities, are turning-points, watersheds of human history. When they flourished in Italy, they brought the age of the Renaissance. So it has been since the city-states, the poleis of ancient Greece, the medinas of the Muslim conquest, to our own times. All major bursts of growth are expressed by an urban explosion.

The fundamental aspects of towns: power, markets, division of labor. Cities were population sinks, drawing in immigrants from the countryside. Lots of poverty, lots of death, lots of abandoned children, lots of old/sick/dying in horrible poor-houses like the Hotel-Dieu

The town was able to try the experiment of leading a completely separate life for quite a long time. This was a colossal event. Its genesis cannot be pinpointed with certainty, but its enormous consequences are visible.

Capitalism and towns were basically the same thing in the West. Lewis Mumford humorously claimed that capitalism was the cuckoo's egg laid in the confined nests of the medieval towns. By this he meant to convey that the bird was destined to grow inordinately and burst its tight framework (which was true), and then link up with the state, the conqueror of towns but heir to their institutions and way of thinking and completely incapable of dispensing with them.

question: Model of why Rome fell:
reference:
State Capacity S = f(Tax surplus, Military effectiveness, Elite cohesion, Information/admin tech)

The Western empire collapses when S falls below the threshold needed to:

defeat or scare off external coalitions at the frontier, and

discourage internal challengers from trying their luck.

Each driver hits S from a different angle:

Fiscal overstretch → lowers Tax surplus; increases cost of marginal security.

Civil war → destroys Elite cohesion; squanders tax base on intra-elite fighting.

Barbarian confederations → increase required S (stronger opponents; internal rivals with armies).

Disease/climate → shrink Tax surplus and recruit pool; increase volatility.

Shifts in elite incentives → reduce willingness to cooperate with the center, so reforms fail.

question: 4 types of defensibility from NFX
reference:
Economies of scale (example: Amazon). When you get bigger, a host of advantages accrue to you. More users means more volume, means you can get cheaper prices from suppliers, means lower prices for customers, means higher conversion rates, makes your advertising more effective than your competition, etc. The numbers all move in your favor, and math is hard to compete with.

Brand (examples: Booking.com, Google). With brand, a certain company can stand top of mind when we think of something we need, like booking.com when I need a hotel room. Priceline, the owner of Booking.com, spends more than $2 billion per year in advertising to make sure that’s true. Further, people come to identify themselves with brands. People who want to associate with Apple products will not comparison shop. Those psychological barriers make it very hard for competitors to break in.

Embedding (examples: Workday, Oracle, SAP). Embedding works when you integrate your software into a customer’s operations so the customer can’t rip you out and replace you with a competitor. This is obviously more prevalent when customers are organizations, not individuals, and is typically accompanied by a direct sales force to drive the embed.

Network effects (examples: LinkedIn, Alibaba, Craigslist). A network effect is when another user makes the service more valuable for every other user. Once your company gets ahead, users won’t find as much value in your competitors’ smaller networks.

question: Issue with main two drug modalities in targeting TFs:
reference:
small molecule drugs, where they're defined just by their size. The reason they have to be small is they need to be small enough to wiggle through the membrane of a cell and get inside. Then you run into a challenge. If you want to actually stick a small molecule between two proteins that have a pretty big interface—meaning they've got big swaths on the side of them that all sort of line up and form a synapse with one another—then you would need a big molecule in order to inhibit that. It turns out that TF's binding DNA is a pretty darn big surface. Small molecules aren't great at disrupting that and certainly even worse at activating it. Small molecules can get all the way into the nucleus, but they can't do much once they're there. They're just too small.

The other classic modalities we have are recombinant proteins. We make a protein like a hormone in a big vat. We grow it in some Chinese hamster ovary cells, we extract it, we inject it into you. This is how, for instance, human insulin works that we make today. Or you make antibodies produced by the immune system. These run around and find proteins that have a particular sequence, they bind to it, and often they just stop it from working by glomming a big thing onto the side. Those are too big to get through the cell membrane. Then they can't actually get to a TF or do anything directly. So we take these bank shots.

question: Feedback loop of polarization:

The media tends to spread more inflammatory content because it is most likely to attract attention. Political elites are incentivized to stoke conflicts to ensure that their voter base remains engaged. Collectively, the news media, social media and elite members of society contribute to institutional polarization.

As a result, ordinary people overestimate division in society. This creates the phenomenon of perceived or false polarization, which often includes the belief that a much larger share of those in the other party hold morally appalling views than they actually do.

In turn, false polarization may intensify dislike for the opponents, which then becomes affective polarization.

This can then exacerbate perceived ideological polarization. Party divides become more stark and people turn blindly loyal to their own side. Individuals may have an increasing emotional sense that the other side is worse, and they cannot possibly agree with their “enemy.”

Finally, ideological polarization can influence politicians to embrace more extremist views and rhetoric, in turn feeding polarizing media (the institutional form mentioned earlier).

question: What is facilitated variation?
reference:
Modular variation of components in development

Organisms are built from a set of highly conserved modules called "core processes" that function in development and physiology, and have remained largely unchanged for millions (in some instances billions) of years. Genetic mutation leads to regulatory changes in the package of core components (i.e. new combinations, amounts, and functional states of those components) exhibited by an organism. Finally, the altered combinations, amounts, and states of the conserved components function to develop and operate a new trait on which natural selection acts. Because of their modular organization, adaptability (e.g. arising through exploratory processes) and compartmentation, developmental systems tend to produce facilitated (i.e. functional and adaptive) phenotypic variation when challenged by genetic mutation or novel environmental conditions.

question: Tasmanian toolkit:
reference:
24 items.
Didn’t even catch fish

When the earliest European explorers made contact with the Tasmanians in the late eighteenth century, they discovered a population of hunter-gatherers equipped with the simplest toolkit of any society ever encountered (by Europeans). To hunt and fight, men used only a one-piece spear, rocks, and throwing clubs. For watercraft, the Tasmanians relied on leaky reed rafts and lacked paddles. To ford rivers, women would swim the raft across, towing their husbands and offspring. In the cool maritime climate, Tasmanians slung wallaby skins over their shoulders and applied grease to their exposed skin. Curiously, the Tasmanians did not catch or eat any fish, despite fish being plentiful around the island. They drank from skulls and may even have lost the ability to make fire. In all, the Tasmanian toolkit consisted of only about twenty-four items.

4. How do the organics on meteorites (or from space more generally) initially form?

Deamer:
reference: The dust particles in the molecular clouds that give rise to stars, solar systems and planets have a thin layer of water ice on the surface mixed with ammonia (NH3), methanol (CH3OH) and carbon monoxide. When UV light from a star illuminates the dust particles, it activates the simple carbon and nitrogen compounds in the ice which undergo a variety of reactions that generate more complex organic compounds. These are carried along with the dust particles when they accrete into planetesimals, comets and asteroids. question: Metaphor for liver vs. kidney vs. spleen:
reference:
1. Liver: The City’s Recycling and Waste Management Center

• The liver is like the city’s recycling and waste management center. It processes nutrients from the food you eat, detoxifies chemicals, and metabolizes drugs. Just as a recycling center sorts and processes different types of waste to be reused or disposed of properly, the liver processes and detoxifies various substances, converting them into forms that the body can use or safely eliminate.

2. Kidneys: The City’s Water Treatment Plant

• The kidneys function like the city’s water treatment plant. They filter out waste products and excess substances from the blood, producing urine to excrete these wastes. Just as a water treatment plant purifies water and ensures clean water supply for the city, the kidneys maintain the balance of water, salts, and minerals in your body, ensuring your internal environment remains stable and clean.

3. Spleen: The City’s Police and Recycling Station

• The spleen is akin to a combination of a police station and a smaller recycling center. It monitors the blood for foreign invaders (like bacteria and viruses) and removes old or damaged red blood cells. Just as police patrol the city to catch criminals and ensure safety, the spleen identifies and helps remove harmful pathogens. Simultaneously, like a recycling station, it breaks down old blood cells and recycles their components.

question: What does shigella do to us?
reference:
Shigella is a bacterium that causes shigellosis, an infection that primarily affects the colon (large intestine). Its effects include:

1. Invasion of Colonic Epithelial Cells: Shigella invades the epithelial cells lining the colon, leading to cell death and ulceration.

2. Inflammation: The invasion triggers a strong immune response, causing inflammation and swelling of the colon.

3. Diarrhea: The infection results in frequent, small-volume stools that may be watery or contain mucus and blood.

4. Cytotoxin Production: Shigella produces Shiga toxin, which damages the intestinal lining and can lead to severe symptoms, including bloody diarrhea.

5. Systemic Symptoms: In severe cases, the toxin can enter the bloodstream, potentially causing systemic effects like hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS), especially in children.

The original transport is UUCP (Unix-to-Unix Copy Protocol) — which is literally just a program for copying files between Unix machines over phone lines. One machine dials another, they exchange batches of new articles, hang up. The "protocol" for which articles to exchange was crude — basically send everything and let the receiver discard duplicates.

NNTP arrives in 1986 as a purpose-built replacement that runs over TCP/IP. It doesn't change what Usenet is — the newsgroup structure, the article format, the social conventions all stay the same. It just replaces the transport underneath.

So Usenet is actually a good case study for your framework — the content layer (newsgroups, articles, threading) stayed constant while the transport layer was swapped out underneath it.

Plants

Fungi

1. Chestnut Blight (Cryphonectria parasitica): Efforts have been made to control the spread of chestnut blight, a fungal disease that devastated American chestnut trees. Biological control and breeding for resistance are ongoing strategies.

question: Other examples of domesticated gas besides steam? (3)
reference:
Gas stoves/lighting, hot air ballons, fridges

Gas lighting (1792–1810s onward) — William Murdoch lit his house with coal gas in 1792. By 1812, London had gas streetlights. This is domesticated gas for light, not work. You heat coal in an enclosed vessel, capture the gas that comes off (mostly methane, hydrogen, carbon monoxide), pipe it to burners. This was the main lighting revolution of the 19th century — electric light didn't overtake gas until the 1900s. Your lighting chart's big drop from 1820–1890 is mostly gas, not electricity.

Hot air balloons (1783) — the Montgolfiers. Heated air is less dense, so it rises. The first human flight. Not mechanically useful, but psychologically enormous — humans left the ground for the first time. Domesticated gas for lift.

Internal combustion (1860s onward) — instead of using fire to boil water to make steam, just explode the fuel inside the cylinder. The expanding combustion gases push the piston directly. More efficient, more compact, eventually kills steam for transport. The Otto cycle (1876) and then the diesel engine (1893). This is domesticated explosion.

Refrigeration (1830s–1850s) — this is the sneaky one. It runs the heat engine backwards. Compress a gas → it heats up → let the heat escape → let the gas expand → it gets cold. You're using gas's phase-change properties to pump heat from one place to another. Jacob Perkins (1834), then commercial ice-making by the 1850s, then refrigerated ships (1880). This changed food completely — it's why Argentine beef could reach London, why you could have fresh milk in cities, why food waste plummeted. Domesticated gas for cold.

question: Why no marketplace emerge in radio/TV?
reference:
No interaction, ephemeral content

No return channel. This is the most fundamental. Broadcast is one-directional by architecture. Even with infinite spectrum, a viewer can't respond through the same medium. To act on something they see, they have to leave the system — pick up a phone, mail a letter. The medium can advertise but it can't close a transaction loop. A marketplace requires two-way communication between participants, and broadcast simply doesn't have that.

Temporal/ephemeral content. Broadcast is linear — it streams past you. You can't browse, search, compare, or return to a listing at your own pace. A marketplace needs persistent, searchable inventory. If a seller's offer aired at 2:14pm and you weren't watching, it's gone. This is the opposite of what matching requires.

Cost was real but secondary. Running a station required serious capital (transmitters, towers, studios, licenses), which concentrated broadcasting power. But even if you handed everyone a cheap transmitter, you'd still have one-way ephemeral signals with no way to match buyers and sellers.

The proof: QVC and the Home Shopping Network were the closest broadcast got to a "marketplace" — and they were really just a televised catalog with phone ordering bolted on. The TV handled the advertising half, but the actual transaction had to escape into a completely different system (telephone + credit card processing). That's not a marketplace, it's an ad channel with a call center.

So the real hierarchy of constraints is probably: one-way architecture > ephemeral content > cost/scarcity.

question: Tiananmen taught the Chinese Communist Party a crucial lesson:
reference:
Tiananmen taught the Chinese Communist Party a crucial lesson: urban unrest is the biggest threat to regime survival. But there's an often-overlooked economic context to those protests - inflation was surging in the late 1980s. This wasn't just a political crisis, it was an economic one.

The inflation happened because of Deng's early reforms: they partially liberalized prices while still maintaining the dual-track system (where some prices were market-based while others remained state-controlled). This created opportunities for arbitrage between the two systems and, combined with rapid credit expansion and wage increases, sent prices soaring. By 1988-89, urban residents were watching their savings and purchasing power evaporate.

So when party leaders looked at Tiananmen's aftermath, they drew two conclusions: first, keep urban residents happy at all costs; second, maintain strict control over prices and financial stability. It's a classic case of economic hardship driving political upheaval.

question: How does matrix factorization work?
reference:
Decompose large sparse matrix into two smaller ones

The idea is that the giant sparse user-item matrix can be decomposed into two smaller matrices — one representing each user as a vector of hidden preferences (latent factors), and one representing each movie as a vector of hidden attributes. Maybe latent factor 1 loosely corresponds to "how artsy vs. mainstream" and factor 2 to "how action-heavy," though the system never labels them — they emerge from the data.

To predict whether you'll like a movie, you take the dot product of your user vector with the movie's vector. If your vectors point in similar directions in this latent space, the model predicts a high rating.

question: How much fusion fuel is on Earth?
reference:
The most likely fuel for nuclear fusion is deuterium that is found in ordinary water. Deuterium accounts for about 0.015% of hydrogen in naturally occuring water, and a small percentage of its mass would be converted into energy in a fusion reaction. However, one liter of ordinary seawater would still produce as much energy in a fusion reaction as 500 liters of fossil fuels in a chemical reaction.

There’s more than a billion cubic kilometers of water on Earth. This means there’s about ten billion times more water than oil, so the water would last five trillion times longer than oil, given constant energy consumption. This means the Sun will burn out long before we would run out of fuel for fusion, making it last “forever” for any practical purposes.

question: What does rotavirus do to us?
reference:
Rotavirus is a leading cause of severe diarrhea in young children. It primarily affects the small intestine, causing the following effects:

1. Infection of Enterocytes: Rotavirus infects and damages the enterocytes, which are the cells lining the small intestine responsible for nutrient absorption.

2. Malabsorption: Damage to these cells leads to malabsorption of nutrients and water.

3. Diarrhea: The infection causes the release of enterotoxins that lead to increased secretion of fluids into the intestine, resulting in watery diarrhea.

4. Inflammation: The immune response to the virus causes inflammation, further contributing to gastrointestinal symptoms like cramping and pain.

question:
Quantify impact of iron on iron age.

Tools:
reference:
2 | Tools: ploughs, sickles and the food surplus

The heavy moldboard plough (iron ploughshare + coulter + mouldboard) could bite, turn and drain the dense clay of northern Europe. Field experiments on modern clay analogues show 15–30 % higher yields versus scratch-ploughing, plus two-thirds less labour.

Economic consequences. A difference-in-difference study of 268 European regions finds the new plough alone explains ≈ 10 % of the spectacular rise in population density and urbanisation between 900-1300 CE.

Chinese parallel. Eastern-Han triple-share iron ploughs let a single farmer till ~4.5 ha/day—about 3 × the area achievable with a wooden ard.

Harvesting kit. Iron sickles could be forged thin, serrated and re-sharpened easily; time-and-motion studies on hand-harvesting cereals report 20-25 % faster output and lower physical strain.

Bottom line: Iron farm tools didn’t just extend acreage—they raised yield per acre and freed labour for crafts, trade and soldiering.

question: Stage 3 of organic life?

The earliest forms of selection, based on relative rates of synthesis and degradation, gave way to proper natural selection, in which populations of protocells with genes and proteins began to compete for survival within vent pores. The standard mechanisms of evolution eventually produced sophisticated proteins in early cells, including ribosomes and the ATP synthase, proteins conserved universally across life today. I envisage that LUCA, the common ancestor of bacteria and archaea, lived within the micropores of alkaline hydrothermal vents. question: Why US polarization in 1800s so low?
reference:
Two dimensions, not one. In the 19th century a lot of the heat (slavery/sectionalism, later civil-rights) lived on the second DW-NOMINATE dimension. The chart you posted tracks only the first (left–right economic) axis, so it understates antebellum/sectional conflict.

Heterogeneous parties. Both parties contained big internal wings (e.g., Southern conservatives inside the Democrats, progressive Republicans in the North). That created lots of cross-party coalitions and roll-call overlap.

Weak nationalization. Politics was more regional and patronage-based; many roll calls were about rivers & harbors, tariffs for specific industries, appointments, etc.—issues that didn’t split cleanly by party.

Restricted electorate. Much of the public was excluded from voting; “mass” affective polarization could stay muted even while elites fought.

Procedural shifts. Stronger party discipline arrives late (e.g., the Reed Rules in the 1890s), which gradually reduced cross-party voting.

Quantify impact of iron on iron age.

Society:
reference:
3 | Societal knock-ons

State power & war-making. Cheap iron kit underwrote large standing armies, siege engines and cavalry gear, shifting dominance from coastal tin-importers (Mycenae, Ugarit) to inland, resource-rich empires (Assyria, Persia).

Demography & cities. The extra calories unlocked by the heavy plough fed a medieval population that nearly tripled, while the 10 % plough-driven slice of that growth helped Europe reach an urbanisation rate > 10 % by 1300.

Economy & class. Blacksmiths became high-status specialists; charcoal demand drove forest management and early regulations; and long-distance tin trade waned, re-routing wealth and political influence.

Environmental cost. Vast iron smelting ate wood for charcoal, accelerating deforestation across Anatolia, the Levant and later Europe.

question: What diff between tabulators, keypunch machines, sorters, and collators? IBM
reference:
Keypunch machines — the data entry point.

Sorters — took a big pile of cards and arranged them into order.

Collators — this is the one that's easy to confuse with sorters. A collator took two already-sorted decks and merged them together, or matched them against each other. This was critical for relational operations. For Social Security, you'd have a master deck of employee records and a new batch of quarterly earnings reports arriving from employers. The collator would interleave the new reports into the right positions alongside each employee's master card.

Tabulators (accounting machines) — the brains of the operation. These actually read the data on cards, performed arithmetic (addition, subtraction, running totals), and printed results. A tabulator could read a sorted deck of purchase cards, subtotal by department, subtotal by vendor, and print a formatted report with all the line items and totals.

Calculate a vector similarity score between each two (i.e. the dot-product similarity in the original paper)

And add the weighted context by weighting their corresponding value vectors.

question: Why does Tyler Cowen think AI take-off is relatively slow?
reference:
Baumol cost disease, human bottlenecks, O-ring, economics not understood, technological diffusion slow, GDP growth 2%, so 0.5% growth

1. Due to the Baumol-Bowen cost disease, less productive sectors tend to become a larger share of the economy over time. This already has been happening since the American economy originated. A big chunk of current gdp already is slow to respond, highly inefficient, governmental or government-subsidized sectors. They just won't adopt AI, or use it effectively, all that quickly. As I said to an AI guy a few days ago "The way I can convince you is to have you sit in on a Faculty Senate meeting." And the more effiicient AI becomes, the more this trend is likely to continue, which slows the prospective measured growth gains from AI.

2. Human bottlenecks become more important, the more productive is AI. Let's say AI increases the rate of good pharma ideas by 10x. Well, until the FDA gets its act together, the relevant constraint is the rate of drug approval, not the rate of drug discovery.

2b. These do not have to be regulatory obstacles, though many are. It may be slow adopters, people in the workplace who hate AI, energy constraints, and much more. It simply is not the case that all workplace inputs are rising in lockstep, quite the contrary.

3. The O-Ring models makes AI hard to work with. The O-Ring model stipulates that, in some settings, it is the worst performer who sets the overall level of productivity. (In the NBA, for instance, it may be the quality of the worst defender on the floor, since the player your worst defender is supposed to guard can just keep taking open shots.) Soon enough, at least in the settings where AI is supposed to shine, the worst performer will be the humans. The AIs will make the humans somewhat better, but not that much better all that quickly.

This is a variant of #2, but in more extreme form. A simple way to put it is that you are not smart enough to notice directly how much better o5 will be than o3. For various complex computational tasks, not observed by humans, the more advanced model of course will be more effective. But when it comes to working with humans, those extra smarts largely will be wasted.

3b. The human IQ-wages gradient is quite modest, suggesting that more IQ in the system does not raise productivity dramatically. You might think that does not hold across the super-intelligent margin the machines will inhabit, but the O-Ring model suggests otherwise, apart from some specialized calculations where the machine does not need to collaborate with humans.

4. I don't think the economics of AI are well-defined by either "an increase in labor supply," "an increase in TFP," or "an increase in capital," though it is some of each of those. It is more like "some Star Trek technology fell into our backyard, and how long will it take us to figure out how to integrate it with other things humans do?" You can debate how long that will take, but the Solow model, the Romer model and their offshoots will not give us reliable answers.

5. There is a vast literature on the diffusion of new technologies (go ask DeepResearch!). Historically it usually takes more time than the most sophisticated observers expect. Electricity for instance arguably took up to forty years. I do think AI will spread faster than that, but reading this literature will bring you back down to earth.

6. Historically, gdp growth is remarkably smooth, albeit for somewhat mysterious reasons. North America is a vastly different place than it was in the year 1600, technologically and otherwise. Yet there are remarkably few years when the economic growth rate is all that far from two percent. There is a Clutch Plague, some years of higher growth, some stagnation, and a few major wars, but even in those cases we are not so far from two percent. I do not pretend to be able to model this satisfactorily (though the above factors surely have relevance in non-AI settings too), but unless you have figured this puzzle out, do not be too confident in any prediction that is so very far from two percent.

7. I've gone on record as suggesting that AI will boost economic growth rates by half a percentage point a year. That is very much a guess. It does mean that, with compounding, the world is very different a few decades out. It also means that year to year non-infovores will not necessarily notice huge changes in their environments. So far I have not seen evidence to contradict that broad expectation.

8. None of these views are based on pessimism about the capabilities of AI models. I hear various views, often from people working in the area, and on the tech per se I have an optimism that corresponds to the weighted average of what I hear.

A particularly illuminating element of the book is how these evolved dispositions have continued to be influential. Nepotism, or kin selection, as expressed in strong tribal or clan lineages, is a continuing theme in the book as the nemesis of the modern state. If tribalism is strong, as today in Afghanistan or the Sunni Triangle of Iraq, modern states cannot flourish.

The importance of religion as an influence on political development is another theme throughout. It was from religion, Fukuyama argues, that the rule of law arose. The key role of norms and institutions provides the subject-matter of the book: political institutions. Fukuyama regards the desire for status or recognition as the main source of change in history, and he engages in a running dispute through the book with rationalist or rational-choice explanations. question: How does infini-attention in an infini-transformer work?
reference:
How Infini-attention works:
• has local attention like any transformer
• has global attention via compression
• combines local and global attention

Regular transformer: discards attention memory of old context windows to free up space for new context.

So if context window is 100K tokens and document is 500K, each of the 5 windows will have new memory.

Memory is lost between windows.

Infini-attention: preserves attention memory of old context windows in compressed key-value states.

So if context window is 100K tokens and document is 500K, all 5 windows have access to entire 500K context.

The attention is compressed in key-value states from all previous windows.

This allows retrieving global context for each window, not just the local context.

Thus enabling infinite context.

question: What does liberalism tell us to want?
reference:
Nothing, so industriousness and consumerism fill the void

Liberalism claims to free people from “artificial” bonds imposed by cultures and distinct local communities that have been deemed oppressive if they infringe on the ability to the Self to do as it wills. Through the power of the state and market, it eradicates or weakens intermediate institutions, including the family, that historically have been tasked with molding human beings in particular directions. Instead, it liberates individuals in order to give untrammeled indulgence to the individual will. Under liberalism, people can and should do what they "want," and should also not be trained in what it is best to “want," which would again be a form of artifice and oppression. question: % of homo sapien calories from megafauna 200,000 to 10,000 years ago:
reference:
33%

1. Early Homo sapiens (~200,000 to 50,000 years ago): During the earlier part of this period, Homo sapiens primarily subsisted on a mix of plant foods, smaller game, and, where available, megafauna. While specific percentages are hard to pin down, megafauna could have contributed between 20-40% of the diet in regions where they were prevalent.

2. Upper Paleolithic (~50,000 to 10,000 years ago): As hunting technologies and strategies improved, the reliance on megafauna increased in many regions. In some areas, particularly in Ice Age Europe and North America, the contribution of megafauna to the diet could have been even higher, potentially accounting for up to 50% or more of the caloric intake. However, this percentage would have varied widely based on local ecology and the availability of other food sources.

3. Regional Variations: In areas where megafauna were less common or absent, such as in some tropical regions, Homo sapiens would have relied more on smaller game, fish, and plant resources, resulting in a lower percentage of calories from megafauna.

4. Decline of Megafauna: By the end of this period (around 10,000 years ago), many megafauna species had become extinct, likely due to a combination of overhunting and climate change. This would have led to a significant shift in dietary patterns toward smaller game and plant-based foods.

In summary, while the specific percentage of calories from megafauna would have varied greatly by time and place, it is reasonable to estimate that megafauna could have contributed anywhere from 20% to over 50% of the caloric intake in regions where these large animals were abundant and heavily relied upon.

question: Secrecy during atomic bomb:
reference:
Szilard made fermi keep graphite secret

He conceived the nuclear chain reaction in 1933, patented the idea in 1936, and in late 1939 wrote the letter for Albert Einstein's signature that resulted in the Manhattan Project that built the atomic bomb.

In the fall of 1940, Fermi had finished new carbon absorption measurements on graphite, suggesting graphite was a viable moderator for a bomb. Szilard assaulted Fermi with yet another secrecy appeal. “At this time Fermi really lost his temper; he really thought this was absurd,” Szilard recounted. Luckily, further appeals were eventually successful, and Fermi reluctantly refrained from publishing his graphite results.

At the same time, the German project had narrowed down on two possible moderator materials: graphite and heavy water. In early 1941 at Heidelberg, Walther Bothe made an incorrect measurement on the absorption cross-section of graphite, and concluded that graphite would absorb too many neutrons to sustain a chain reaction. Since Fermi had kept his result secret, the Germans did not have Fermi’s measurements to check against, and to correct the error. This was crucial: it led the German project to pursue heavy water instead—a decisive wrong path that ultimately doomed the German nuclear weapons effort.

question: Denominations created by Four Great Awakenings:
reference:
First Great Awakening (1730s–1740s) Congregationalists and Presbyterians

Second Great Awakening (1790s–1840s) Methodists and Baptists on the frontier, and Mormons and “voluntary societies” (abolition, etc.)

Third Great Awakening (1850s–early 1900s): Social Gospel holiness and mission movements (feedstock for later Pentecostalism), parachurch YMCA etc

Fourth Great Awakening (mid-20th century–present) evangelicalism, charismatic/Pentecostal, Religious Right

///

First Great Awakening (1730s–1740s) formed/accelerated: “New Light” factions within Congregationalists and Presbyterians (e.g., New Side Presbyterians), rapid growth of Baptists (especially “Separate Baptists”), and a broader intercolonial evangelical network (revival itinerants + new revival-friendly colleges).

Second Great Awakening (1790s–1840s) formed/accelerated: Major expansion of Methodists and Baptists on the frontier, new restorationist groups like the Disciples of Christ / Stone–Campbell movement, new American-born movements like the Latter-day Saints (Mormons), and a dense ecosystem of reform and “voluntary societies” (abolition, temperance, missions, Bible/school societies).

Third Great Awakening (1850s–early 1900s) formed/accelerated: The Social Gospel and institutional reform Christianity (settlement houses, urban missions), the modern holiness and mission movements (feedstock for later Pentecostalism), and large national parachurch-style organizations (e.g., mass evangelism, YMCA/Student Volunteer–type mobilization).

Fourth Great Awakening (mid-20th century–present; debated) formed/accelerated: Modern evangelicalism as a cohesive public identity (megachurch + media ministries), the charismatic/Pentecostal surge into mainline churches, and explicitly political formations like the Religious Right (issue-based coalitions and advocacy organizations).

Hurricanes, typhoons and whirlpools are all striking natural examples of dissipative structures. We find them on a vast scale in the oceans and atmosphere too, driven by the differences in energy flux from the sun at the equator relative to the poles. Reliable ocean currents, such as the Gulf Stream, and winds, such as the Roaring Forties or the North Atlantic jet stream, are not specified by information, but are as stable and continuous as the energy flux that sustains them. The Great Red Spot of Jupiter is a huge storm, an anticyclone several times the size of the earth, which has persisted for at least a few hundred years. Just as the convection cells in a kettle persist for as long as the electric current keeps the water boiling and steam evaporating, all these dissipative structures require a continuous flux of energy. In more general terms, they are the visible products of sustained far-from-equilibrium conditions, in which energy flux maintains a structure indefinitely, until at last (after billions of years in the case of stars) equilibrium is attained and the structure finally collapses. The main point is that sustained and predictable physical structures can be produced by energy

question: Nick Lane explanation of chlorophyll photosynthesis:
reference:
When chlorophyll absorbs a photon, its internal bonds are energized. The energetic vibrations force an electron from the molecule, leaving the chlorophyll short of one electron. Loss of an electron creates an unstable reactive form of chlorophyll. However, the newly reactive molecule cannot simply take back its missing electron. That is snatched by a neighbouring protein and is whipped off down a chain of linked –proteins, putting it beyond reach, like a rugby ball being passed across the field by a line of players. On the way, its energy Is used to power the synthesis of ATP in a manner exactly analogous to that in mitochondrial respiration.

The theft of an electron is half way to stealing an entire hydrogen atom as hydrogen consists of a single proton and a single electron. Little extra work is needed to steal the proton. Electrostatic rearrangements draw a positively charged proton (from water in the case of oxygenic photosynthesis) after the negatively charged electron. The proton and electron are eventually reunited by Rubisco as a hydrogen atom in a sugar molecule.

What happens to the chlorophyll? Having lost an electron, it becomes far more reactive, and will snatch an electron from the nearest suitable source. Reactive chlorophyll is constrained in the same way as a mediaeval dragon which is fed with virgins to stop it ravaging the neighborhood. The source of suitable-virgins — electrons in the case of chlorophyll — includes any plentiful sacrificial chemical, such as water, hydrogen sulphide or iron. Devouring an electron settles the chlorophyll back into its normal equable state, at least until another photon sets the whole cycle in motion again

question: The unprecedented success of the Neo-Assyrian Empire was due to:

As the first of its scale, the empire saw various military, civic and administrative innovations. In the military, important innovations included a large-scale use of cavalry and new siege warfare techniques. Techniques first adopted by the Neo-Assyrian army would be used in later warfare for millennia.[17] To solve the issue of communicating over vast distances, the empire developed a sophisticated state communication system, using relay stations and well-maintained roads. The communication speed of official messages in the empire was not surpassed in the Middle East until the 19th century.[22][23] The empire also made use of a resettlement policy, wherein some portions of the populations from conquered lands were resettled in the Assyrian heartland and in underdeveloped provinces. This policy served to both disintegrate local identities and to introduce Assyrian-developed agricultural techniques to all parts of the empire. A consequence was the dilution of the cultural diversity of the Near East, forever changing the ethnolinguistic composition of the region and facilitating the rise of Aramaic as the regional lingua franca,[24] a position the language retained until the 14th century.[25]

question:
Word Embedding
vs.
Attention Mechanism
reference:
Word Embeddings are high-dimensional vector representations of words that capture their semantic and syntactic properties. These representations enable the model to numerically manipulate words in a mathematical space, a sort of semantic space, where physically nearby words share some form of relationship of meaning or other kinds of similarities. Instead of treating words as isolated entities, word embeddings allow the model to learn and understand the complex interplay of words within a given context.

Attention Mechanisms allow the model to weigh the importance of different words or phrases in the text. This helps the model to selectively focus on specific parts of the input, assigning different attention scores to the words based on their relevance to the task at hand. Attention can be thought of as a numerical operation that is supposed to mimic the “focusing ability” of a model to the local, specific context as it reads through or generates text.

question: What is shard theory in AI?
reference:
Cultural evolution behind how we got values.

A shard of value refers to the contextually activated computations which are downstream of similar historical reinforcement events. For example, the juice-shard consists of the various decision-making influences which steer the baby towards the historical reinforcer of a juice pouch. These contextual influences were all reinforced into existence by the activation of sugar reward circuitry upon drinking juice. A subshard is a contextually activated component of a shard. For example, “IF juice pouch in front of me THEN grab” is a subshard of the juice-shard. It seems plain to us that learned value shards are[5] most strongly activated in the situations in which they were historically reinforced and strengthened. (For more on terminology, see Appendix A.2.)

question: Titans vs. Nested Learning:
reference:
Imagine an AI that doesn't just learn new facts, but actively learns how to learn better...

(Baldwin effect)

and then learns how to get better at learning how to learn better, and so on, in an infinite loop.

The Old Way (Titans)

What it is: Think of "Titans" as an AI with a really smart to-do list for its memory.

How it works: It pays attention to everything happening. If something surprising or unexpected occurs, it flags that memory as "important" and stores it long-term. Less surprising stuff gets forgotten. This is a powerful way to manage memory.

The Problem: The way it decides what is "surprising" is fixed. It has its learning rules (Level 1) and it can update its memory based on those rules (Level 2), but it can't step back and change the rules themselves. It's called "first-order" learning because it can't question its own fundamental learning strategy.

The New Way (Hope)

What it is: "Hope" is a new design that uses a concept called "Nested Learning."

How it works: Hope is "self-modifying." It can look at its own performance and literally rewrite its own parameters (its "learning rules") based on what it just learned.

The "Infinite Loop": This creates "unbounded levels" of learning:

Level 1: It learns a new fact (e.g., "This user likes short answers").

Level 2: It reviews its own learning (e.g., "I learned that fact, and it's now in my memory").

Level 3: It then optimizes its learning strategy (e.g., "My process for learning user preferences is good, but it's too slow. I will change my own code to make this process faster next time.").

Level 4: It can then review that change... and so on, forever. It's "self-referential" because it's constantly looking at itself to find ways to improve its own core architecture.

question: Five clusters of AI risk from Richard Ngo:
reference:
MIRI cluster. Think that P(doom) is very high, based on intuitions about instrumental convergence, deceptive alignment, etc. Does work that's very different from mainstream ML. Central members: Eliezer Yudkowsky, Nate Soares.

Structural risk cluster. Think that doom is more likely than not, but not for the same reasons as the MIRI cluster. Instead, this cluster focuses on systemic risks, multi-agent alignment, selective forces outside gradient descent, etc. Often work that's fairly continuous with mainstream ML, but willing to be unusually speculative by the standards of the field. Central members: Dan Hendrycks, David Krueger, Andrew Critch.

Constellation cluster. More optimistic than either of the previous two clusters. Focuses more on risk from power-seeking AI than the structural risk cluster, but does work that is more speculative or conceptually-oriented than mainstream ML. Central members: Paul Christiano, Buck Shlegeris, Holden Karnofsky. (Named after Constellation coworking space.)

Prosaic cluster. Focuses on empirical ML work and the scaling hypothesis, is typically skeptical of theoretical or conceptual arguments. Short timelines in general. Central members: Dario Amodei, Jan Leike, Ilya Sutskever.

Mainstream cluster. Alignment researchers who are closest to mainstream ML. Focuses much less on backchaining from specific threat models and more on promoting robustly valuable research. Typically more concerned about misuse than misalignment, although worried about both. Central members: Scott Aaronson, David Bau.

question: Doesn't epsilon have something to do with the speed that the weak interaction turns protons into neutrons? Isn't that the actual gating factor on hydrogen fusion? (That the weak force happens "slowly".)
reference:
In other words:

\varepsilon (the 0.007) is about how much energy you get out of each fusion reaction (and thus how much mass is lost).

The speed (or probability) of that reaction, especially the first p+p step, is controlled by the weak force, since flipping a proton to a neutron is a weak interaction process.

Why They’re Both Important

If \varepsilon were bigger or smaller (i.e., if the strong force changed enough to alter helium’s binding energy significantly), then fusing four protons into helium could yield much more or much less net energy. That would reshape stellar nucleosynthesis dramatically.

If the weak force were stronger (making that proton-to-neutron flip faster), stars would burn hydrogen more quickly—possibly finishing their main-sequence lives in a fraction of the time.

If the weak force were weaker still, the limiting step would become extremely rare, leading to correspondingly slow fusion (and potentially different stellar structures or even difficulties getting any fusion started).

Physicists tend to focus on \varepsilon (the mass-fraction release) when discussing “fine-tuning” because it’s a dimensionless parameter directly tied to nuclear binding via the strong force. The “slowness” of the weak interaction is also crucial—it determines the Sun’s long lifetime—but that’s typically viewed as a rate (cross section) rather than a dimensionless fraction like 0.007. Both effects, however, are intimately involved in giving stars (and life) the conditions we see.

🤝 Treaty of Ghent (1814):

No territory changed hands.

No mention of the causes of war (impressment, trade interference).

Both sides basically agreed to go back to how things were before the war.

🏆 So… who “won”?

Strategically: Britain was focused on Napoleon; the U.S. held its own, which felt like a win.

question: Song learning in songbirds provides one of the best-understood examples of biological reinforcement learning:
reference:
Young birds learn their songs by listening to more experienced tutors, storing an internal template, or memory, of what the song should sound like based on the tutor song, and then practicing producing their own songs thousands of times while their brains generate error signals by comparing the sound of their outputs with that of the stored template.

Dopamine neurons in the songbird brain fire precisely when a sung note is closer to — or further from — from the tutor song. More interestingly, these reward signals change with social context: When practicing alone, feedback is sharp and corrective, but when singing to a mate, the same circuits suppress error signals, freezing the learned performance. In other words, the bird has an innate instinct that makes it want to copy the songs of older birds.

question: Ravitch is against choice, accountability, and standards. She's in favor of:
reference:
Broad curriculum and supporting teachers

1. A Broad, Well-Rounded Curriculum

• Ravitch maintains that students should engage with literature, history, science, the arts, physical education, and more. Instead of narrowing instruction to what will appear on standardized tests, she believes children need a varied curriculum that fosters critical thinking and creativity.

2. Strengthening Public Schools

• Rather than dismissing “failing” public schools or turning them into privately managed charters, Ravitch emphasizes investing in and improving neighborhood public schools. She highlights the need for resources, smaller class sizes, and support services—especially for students facing poverty, language barriers, or disabilities.

3. Elevating and Supporting Teachers

• Ravitch advocates for treating teachers as professionals. This involves better preparation, mentoring, and ongoing professional development—not simply judging them by how well their students score on standardized exams.

4. Equity and Adequate Resources

• A key theme in Ravitch’s shift is that high-stakes testing punishes the most vulnerable students and schools. She calls for equitable funding, social services, and community support so that all children—particularly those in impoverished areas—have the tools they need to succeed.

5. Local Engagement and Democracy

• Rather than a centralized, test-driven system, Ravitch encourages democratic engagement: parents, teachers, and community members should play an active role in shaping their schools. Overemphasizing national standards, in her view, can hinder local solutions that meet community needs.

question: 8 things I control as a delegator?
reference:
8 things that you control as a delegator
1. The way you give & encourage feedback

Being a masterful delegator means having an effective, fulfilling, and consistent feedback loop with your EA.

Here’s what that looks like:

You and your EA know how each other like to give and receive feedback, and you take care to honor those preferences.

You praise in public, correct in private.

You give feedback immediately & at regular intervals.

You follow the 80/20 principle - 80% positive, 20% constructive tactical.

When giving constructive feedback, you’re specific and you limit your focus.

2. Understanding your EA’s project, task, and knowledge management system and making sure that they work for you.

You and your EA have a system for breaking your goals into systems, rituals, and tasks.

Over 50% of your EA’s work is recurring in some fashion.

3. Knowing what’s important to your EA, the names of the people they care about most, and what their personal goals are.

Consider reserving the first 5 minutes of your next 1:1 sync to ask your EA about their personal goals, wishes, and the key stake holders in their lives.

4. Taking care to know and capitalize on your EA’s strengths and interests.

The most masterful delegators know that the more time people spend in their zone of genius, the higher their output. They are extremely cognizant what their EA’s genuinely enjoy working on and feel inspired to own, and are always on the look out for how they can connect more of their EA’s day to these things.

5. Prioritizing your 1:1 syncs

I can’t tell you how much EAs appreciate this, as well as how much faster they grow as EAs when they have steady time with their clients.

6. Putting emphasis into mentoring your EA, and acknowledging their growth whenever you notice it

As Michael Fertik says in his Harvard Business Review article, “Younger people are especially hungry both to learn and to receive affirmation that they are doing a good job. I’ve found the best ones are generally much more motivated by incremental education and acknowledgement than they are by a modest bump in salary.” You can read my key take aways from his article here.

7. Making sure that your EA truly understands your long term goals, and can connect their daily work back to it.

Making a difference in your life is your EA’s career. One of the primary reasons that they applied for Athena is because they want to meaningfully impact and uplift a leader who inspires them. The more often you contextualize their daily tasks with the purpose that each one serves, the more motivated and fulfilled your EA will be.

8. How clear your instructions are

As our brilliant client, Masha Krol (founder of Glowstick says), practice “zero context delegation.” In other words, as a experiment in developing crystal clarity as a delegator, imagine that the person you’re requesting something from has little to no context on what successful completion of the request looks like in your eyes.

question: How does Lenacapavir work?

Capsid inhibitor. Lenacapavir is a long-acting, potent inhibitor of the HIV capsid protein with in vitro activity against viral strains resistant to other ARV classes. By targeting HIV capsid, lenacapavir interferes with multiple early- to late-stage processes of the viral life cycle: nuclear transport, virus assembly and release, and capsid assembly.5

Lenacapavir binds directly to HIV capsid in a pocket between capsid protein subunits in hexamers. In early stages of the virus life cycle, lenacapavir interferes with capsid-mediated nuclear import of HIV-1 proviral DNA, as it targets the same capsid binding site utilized by host factors that aid in viral nuclear import and integration. In late stages of the HIV life cycle, lenacapavir interferes with the functioning of Gag/Gag-Pol and reduces capsid protein subunit production. question: Why do people like cyanosulfidic networks?
reference:
Lab evidence now spans both genetics and metabolism.

– Cyanosulfidic network (2015–2023) makes ribonucleotide and amino-acid precursors from HCN + HS⁻/SO₃²⁻ under UV.

– Carboxysulfidic sequel (2023–25) converts CO₂ + SO₃²⁻ to citrate, malate, succinate, tartrate at ≥1 mM.

The same solvated-electron photochemistry underlies both halves, knitting “genes first” and “metabolism first” into one flow.

Geochemical plausibility sharpened.

Impact plasmas → ferrocyanide beds; volcanic SO₂ → sulfite lakes; young-Sun UVA flux adequate. These form a coherent, surface-accessible niche that can be falsified by Mars & Archaean strata.

Quantitative yields beat vent formate syntheses by 3–5 orders of magnitude, and the UV requirement is no longer viewed as a bug: recent modelling shows >280 nm photons penetrate even a hazy Hadean sky.

Bridges to modern biochemistry sketched.

– Crystallization of ribose-amino-oxazoline offers a route to homochirality.

– A single promiscuous hydroxy-acid dehydratase could spin the photochemical C₂–C₄ acids into a full proto-Krebs loop.

– Nitrogen still needs to be inserted (transamination of oxaloacetate/α-KG), but the gap is narrower than for pure CO₂-vent schemes.

question: Dario on AI neuroscience:
reference:
In summary, AI-accelerated neuroscience is likely to vastly improve treatments for, or even cure, most mental illness as well as greatly expand “cognitive and mental freedom” and human cognitive and emotional abilities. It will be every bit as radical as the improvements in physical health described in the previous section. Perhaps the world will not be visibly different on the outside, but the world as experienced by humans will be a much better and more humane place, as well as a place that offers greater opportunities for self-actualization. I also suspect that improved mental health will ameliorate a lot of other societal problems, including ones that seem political or economic.

Traditional molecular biology, chemistry, and genetics. This is essentially the same story as general biology in section 1, and AI can likely speed it up via the same mechanisms. There are many drugs that modulate neurotransmitters in order to alter brain function, affect alertness or perception, change mood, etc., and AI can help us invent many more. AI can probably also accelerate research on the genetic basis of mental illness.

Fine-grained neural measurement and intervention. This is the ability to measure what a lot of individual neurons or neuronal circuits are doing, and intervene to change their behavior. Optogenetics and neural probes are technologies capable of both measurement and intervention in live organisms, and a number of very advanced methods (such as molecular ticker tapes to read out the firing patterns of large numbers of individual neurons) have also been proposed and seem possible in principle.

Advanced computational neuroscience. As noted above, both the specific insights and the gestalt of modern AI can probably be applied fruitfully to questions in systems neuroscience, including perhaps uncovering the real causes and dynamics of complex diseases like psychosis or mood disorders.

Behavioral interventions. I haven’t much mentioned it given the focus on the biological side of neuroscience, but psychiatry and psychology have of course developed a wide repertoire of behavioral interventions over the 20th century; it stands to reason that AI could accelerate these as well, both the development of new methods and helping patients to adhere to existing methods. More broadly, the idea of an “AI coach” who always helps you to be the best version of yourself, who studies your interactions and helps you learn to be more effective, seems very promising.

question: What are the 10 things in Built to Move? (5)
reference:
Hips, shoulders, food, sleep, balance

Get Up and Down Off the Floor — Sit-and-Rise Test. Can you go from standing to sitting cross-legged on the floor and back up without using your hands or knees? Scored out of 10. Predicts longevity.

Breathe Easy — Breath-Hold Test (BOLT). After a normal exhale, how long can you hold before the urge to breathe? Tests CO2 tolerance and breathing efficiency. Nose breathing, not mouth.

Extend Your Hips — Can you achieve full hip extension? Modern sitting locks us in hip flexion all day. Couch stretch territory. Glute activation.

Walk This Way — 8,000-10,000 steps daily. Not exercise — just total movement throughout the day. All steps count.

Future-Proof Your Neck and Shoulders — Shoulder rotation and overhead range of motion tests. Can you raise your arms fully overhead with back against a wall? Mobilizations for thoracic spine and rotator cuff.

Eat Like You're Going to Live Forever — Two-part: eat 800 grams of fruits and vegetables daily (~6 cups), and 0.7-1g protein per pound of bodyweight.

Squat — Can you get into a full deep squat, hip crease below knees, and hold for five breaths? Tests hip, knee, and ankle range simultaneously.

Find Your Balance — Stand on one leg, eyes closed. Can you put on shoes and socks standing on one foot? Balance degrades silently and predicts fall risk.

Create a Movement-Rich Environment — Sitting inventory. Spend no more than 6 hours per day in a chair. Standing desk, floor sitting, varied positions throughout the day. This is the Bowman-influenced chapter.

Unleash Your Superpower: Sleep — 7+ hours per night. They consider this the most important of all ten — everything else flows from it.

question: The Gulf War, or: What a few-decades-worth of technological lead implies for military power:
reference:
Same numbers, 4:1 defender advantage, but 300 troops lost to 30k (100x) in 100-hour war

The Gulf War provides a helpful illustration of how a 20-30 year lead in military technology can be decisive. At the time, Iraq commanded the fourth-largest army in the world. In terms of numbers (troops, tanks, artillery), the US-led coalition barely matched (or was outmatched) by the Iraqis, all while the Iraqis had had ample time to entrench their defenses (a situation that would normally require a 3:1, or 5:1, advantage in military manpower to dislocate).

But the US-led coalition obliterated the Iraqi army in a merely 100-hour ground war. Coalition dead numbered a mere 292, compared to 20k-50k Iraqi dead and hundreds of thousands of others wounded or captured. The Coalition lost a mere 31 tanks, compared to the destruction of over 3,000 Iraqi tanks.

The difference in technology wasn’t godlike or unfathomable, but it was utterly and completely decisive: guided and smart munitions, early versions of stealth, better sensors, better tank scopes (to see farther in the night and in dust storms), better fighter jets, an advantage in reconnaissance, and so on.

(For a more recent example, recall Iran launching a massive attack of 300 missiles at Israel, “99%” of which were intercepted by superior Israel, US, and allied missile defense.)

question: US policy options for AI safety? (3)
reference:
Track hardware, software, harms

Software export controls. Control the export (to anyone) of “frontier AI models,” i.e. models with highly general capabilities over some threshold, or (more simply) models trained with a compute budget over some threshold (e.g. as much compute as $1 billion can buy today). This will help limit the proliferation of the models which probably pose the greatest risk. Also restrict API access in some ways, as API access can potentially be used to generate an optimized dataset sufficient to train a smaller model to reach performance similar to that of the larger model.

Require hardware security features on cutting-edge chips. Security features on chips can be leveraged for many useful compute governance purposes, e.g. to verify compliance with export controls and domestic regulations, monitor chip activity without leaking sensitive IP, limit usage (e.g. via interconnect limits), or even intervene in an emergency (e.g. remote shutdown). These functions can be achieved via firmware updates to already-deployed chips, though some features would be more tamper-resistant if implemented on the silicon itself in future chips.

Track stocks and flows of cutting-edge chips, and license big clusters. Chips over a certain capability threshold (e.g. the one used for the October 2022 export controls) should be tracked, and a license should be required to bring together large masses of them (as required to cost-effectively train frontier models). This would improve government visibility into potentially dangerous clusters of compute. And without this, other aspects of an effective compute governance regime can be rendered moot via the use of undeclared compute.

Track and require a license to develop frontier AI models. This would improve government visibility into potentially dangerous AI model development, and allow more control over their proliferation. Without this, other policies like the information security requirements below are hard to implement.

Information security requirements. Require that frontier AI models be subject to extra-stringent information security protections (including cyber, physical, and personnel security), including during model training, to limit unintended proliferation of dangerous models.

Testing and evaluation requirements. Require that frontier AI models be subject to extra-stringent safety testing and evaluation, including some evaluation by an independent auditor meeting certain criteria.[5]

Fund specific genres of alignment, interpretability, and model evaluation R&D. Note that if the genres are not specified well enough, such funding can effectively widen (rather than shrink) the gap between cutting-edge AI capabilities and available methods for alignment, interpretability, and evaluation. See e.g. here for one possible model.

Fund defensive information security R&D, again to help limit unintended proliferation of dangerous models. Even the broadest funding strategy would help, but there are many ways to target this funding to the development and deployment pipeline for frontier AI models.

Create a narrow antitrust safe harbor for AI safety & security collaboration. Frontier-model developers would be more likely to collaborate usefully on AI safety and security work if such collaboration were more clearly allowed under antitrust rules. Careful scoping of the policy would be needed to retain the basic goals of antitrust policy.

Require certain kinds of AI incident reporting, similar to incident reporting requirements in other industries (e.g. aviation) or to data breach reporting requirements, and similar to some vulnerability disclosure regimes. Many incidents wouldn’t need to be reported publicly, but could be kept confidential within a regulatory body. The goal of this is to allow regulators and perhaps others to track certain kinds of harms and close-calls from AI systems, to keep track of where the dangers are and rapidly evolve mitigation mechanisms.

Clarify the liability of AI developers for concrete AI harms, especially clear physical or financial harms, including those resulting from negligent security practices. A new framework for AI liability should in particular address the risks from frontier models carrying out actions. The goal of clear liability is to incentivize greater investment in safety, security, etc. by AI developers.

Create means for rapid shutdown of large compute clusters and training runs. One kind of “off switch” that may be useful in an emergency is a non-networked power cutoff switch for large compute clusters. As far as I know, most datacenters don’t have this.[6] Remote shutdown mechanisms on chips (mentioned above) could also help, though they are vulnerable to interruption by cyberattack. Various additional options could be required for compute clusters and training runs beyond particular thresholds.

question: Overview of US geologic history:
reference:
The geologic history of the United States is quite diverse and complex, but here is a simplified overview:

### Precambrian (before 541 million years ago)

- **Formation of Ancient Crust**: The oldest rocks in the US are found in the Canadian Shield, which extends into parts of northern Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan. These rocks are over 2.5 billion years old and primarily consist of ancient igneous and metamorphic rocks.

### Paleozoic Era (541-252 million years ago)

- **Appalachian Mountains**: During this era, the eastern US was dominated by shallow seas where sediments accumulated and eventually formed sedimentary rocks like sandstone, limestone, and shale. The collision of continental plates led to the formation of the Appalachian Mountains.

- **Interior Seaway**: The central part of North America was covered by a shallow sea, leading to extensive deposits of limestone and other sedimentary rocks.

### Mesozoic Era (252-66 million years ago)

- **Rocky Mountains Formation**: This era saw significant tectonic activity, including the formation of the Rocky Mountains due to the collision and subduction of tectonic plates. This resulted in the uplift and exposure of older rocks.

- **Sedimentary Basins**: Large sedimentary basins formed in places like the Great Plains, where thick sequences of sedimentary rocks accumulated.

### Cenozoic Era (66 million years ago to present)

- **Basin and Range Province**: In the western US, the crust was stretched and thinned, creating a series of north-south trending mountain ranges and valleys known as the Basin and Range Province. This area includes parts of Nevada, Utah, and Arizona, with various types of sedimentary, igneous, and metamorphic rocks.

- **Volcanic Activity**: The Cascades in the Pacific Northwest and the Yellowstone region have significant volcanic activity. The Cascades are part of the Pacific Ring of Fire, formed by subduction of oceanic plates.

- **Coastal Plains**: The Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains are characterized by younger sedimentary rocks deposited by rivers and coastal processes.

### Rock Types and Formation

- **Igneous Rocks**: Found mainly in the western US and parts of the Appalachian region, formed from cooling magma or lava.

- **Sedimentary Rocks**: Widespread across the US, especially in areas that were once covered by seas or large lakes, formed from the accumulation of sediments.

- **Metamorphic Rocks**: Common in the Appalachian Mountains and parts of the western US, formed from the alteration of existing rocks due to heat and pressure.

This overview covers the major geologic events and rock types in the US. The landscape we see today is a result of these processes and the ongoing movement of Earth's tectonic plates.

reference:
Keypunch (031): Operators transcribe employer wage reports onto cards. One card per worker per quarter. ~600K cards/day at peak.

Verify: Second operator re-keys same data on verifier machine to catch transcription errors.

Sort (080): Arrange new quarterly cards by SSN. 9-digit number = 9 passes through the sorter, one column at a time, right to left.

Collate (077): Merge new sorted quarterly cards with existing master file (one summary card per worker). Matches on SSN. Rejects unmatched cards for investigation.

Tabulate (405): Reads matched pairs (master + new quarterly cards), adds new wages to cumulative total, punches updated master card. Also calculates benefits at retirement.

Reproduce: Updated master cards become new master file. Cycle repeats every quarter.

That second factor is often underappreciated. Moore's Law gets all the credit, but a big chunk of the performance story is Dennard scaling (higher clocks at same power) and microarchitectural improvements that let you do more useful work per transistor per cycle. question: Some things David Perell believes about the education system:
reference:
1. Parents say they care about learning, but credentials are really what they value.

2. Education should feel more like a video game than a movie. The current system forces kids to sit back and listen. Better to gamify the experience and make it interactive.

3. Poor pedagogy is a bigger problem than a lack of funding.

4. If teaching kids was the real priority, schools would look a lot different from how they look today.

5. To teach critical thinking, have students argue for perspectives they disagree with and expose their writing to criticism so they have to defend their core beliefs.

6. A major blindspot in education is that the people running the system see the value in learning, so they assume students do too. And so, not enough energy goes into motivating students to learn in the first place.

7. Homework should be the exception, not the rule. Kids are forced to do it every day because the time they spend in school is so unfocused and unproductive.

8. The biggest problem with writing education is teaching kids that good writing comes from big words and long papers.

9. Sorting kids by grade-level works on the playground, but not in the classroom, where kids should be sorted by skill-level. If the material is too easy, they won't learn anything. If it's too hard, they check out. Meet kids where they are (adaptive learning apps are the only way to do this at scale).

10. Almost every kid is absolutely obsessed with something, and if you can frame their studies through the lens of whatever it is, they’ll learn much faster.

11. If you’re trying to build something ambitious in education, get the parents of wealthy children to fund it by building an ultra-high-end product for them. If your product works, they’ll pay exorbitant amounts of money for their kids’ education, and you can use the high profit margin to build a solution for the masses. Elon Musk is doing this with Tesla. Schools can do the same.

12. The modern education system is designed for girls, not boys. Just look at the trends in college graduation rates.

13. The problem with school isn’t the system itself. Rather, the problem is that every school basically teaches people to learn in the same way. Kids around the country are stuck learning at the same speed, with the same tools, and in the same ways.

14. One of the great tragedies of the education system is how many students graduate thinking that learning is boring.

15. The best teachers are increasingly on the Internet, and they're already making millions of dollars per year.

16. 1-on-1 tutoring is the best way to learn. But until recently, it was too expensive and people-intensive to scale to the masses. AI and learning apps have changed that.

17. We are wrong to throw so much shade at the Liberal Arts, but right to criticize the politicization of them. The stories, ideas, and art at the core of Western civilization are the seeds of tremendous wisdom. We should relish them.

18. The idea that it's cool to get good grades without trying hard is a cultural weed that infects nearly every K-12 school in America.

question: in almost every decade of the twentieth century, there was an educational crisis:
reference:
In the early decades, critics said the schools were too academic and were failing to prepare students for an industrial economy. Their loud complaints produced the first significant federal education legislation, the Smith-Lever Act of 1914 and the Smith-Hughes Act of 1917, to promote vocational education.

In the 1930s, critics complained that the schools were failing to meet the needs of youth or of the economy, and federal programs were created (the Civilian Conservation Corps and the National Youth Administration) to fill the gap.

In the 1940s, critics complained that the schools were underfunded, overcrowded, and unprepared for the postwar economy and the atomic age.

In the early 1950s, critics assailed the schools for their lack of academic rigor. Then, when the Soviets launched Sputnik in 1957, public figures and the media blamed the schools for losing the space race and jeopardizing the nation’s security. In response, Congress passed the National Defense Education Act of 1958.

In the 1960s, the nation “discovered” poverty, and the schools were again subject to searing criticism because they reflected the prejudices of the larger society. Congress reacted with the Civil Rights Act of 1964, banning racial discrimination in the schools and other public institutions.

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, the schools were lambasted by critics who discerned, as author Charles Silberman put it, a “crisis in the classroom” due to “mindlessness” and the routinization of education. In response came a flurry of pedagogical experiments, such as open classrooms and student freedom to select their own curriculum.

In 1983, a federal commission declared that the United States was “a nation at risk” because of the failings of our schools. Since the late 1990s, the crisis in education has centered on the achievement gap between children of different races.

Ravitch, Diane. The Death and Life of the Great American School System: How Testing and Choice Are Undermining Education (pp. 297-298). Basic Books. Kindle Edition.

question: 1956 Robert Solow wrote a paper suggesting growth would eventually slow down:
reference: His basic point was that as per capita GDP goes up, people save more, and therefore there is more money to invest, and more capital available per worker. This makes capital less productive; if there are now two machines in a factory where there was only one, the same workers will have to operate both at the same time. Of course, a single factory can hire more workers if it gets more machines. But the whole economy cannot (assuming migration remains unchanged), once its reserve of underused workers is exhausted. Therefore, the extra machines bought with the additional savings will have to be worked with fewer workers. Each new machine and as a consequence each additional unit of capital will contribute less and less to GDP. Growth will slow down. Furthermore, the lower productivity of capital lowers its financial return, which in turn discourages savings. So eventually people will stop saving and growth will slow down.
